title: State
summary: Replace conditionals on a status field with objects that own allowed transitions.

parts.rule: State moves behavior that depends on an object's current mode into state-specific types behind one interface. The context delegates an event to its current state and installs the next state only after a valid transition. Use it when a lifecycle has several modes, repeated conditional logic, and meaningful invalid transitions.
parts.why: A status enum is not a problem by itself. Trouble starts when controllers, services, and UI code each switch on that status and implement different transition rules. State objects put behavior and transition decisions together. They add types and indirection, so a small transition table may still be clearer as one explicit switch.
parts.example: Order 1001 begins Pending. pay(6000 cents) in Pending records payment and transitions to Paid. ship(\"TRACK-9\") in Paid records the tracking number and transitions to Shipped. ship() in Pending returns InvalidTransition before calling the carrier. cancel() is allowed in Pending; in Paid it first requests a refund; in Shipped it is rejected because a return flow is required instead. Each state handles the same events but gives mode-specific results, and the Order context owns shared data such as id and total. Trace the happy path: Pending.pay → Paid.ship → Shipped. Trace a bad path: Pending.ship leaves the order Pending and produces no shipping side effect. If state is persisted as a status column, loading the order must restore the matching state object before the next event. A simple switch inside Order.handle(event) can express these four states well; move to separate state types when the handlers grow, vary independently, or are repeated elsewhere. This differs from Strategy: a caller usually chooses a sorting or pricing strategy, while an Order changes state because events occur during its own lifecycle.
parts.use: Use State for protocols, workflow engines, order or document lifecycles, and UI modes where the same event means different things in different modes. Write the transition table first, make invalid moves explicit, and keep side effects coordinated with the state change so failures do not leave a false status.
parts.refuse: Keep a boolean or enum when two modes have one small conditional. Do not create a class for every flag combination. Avoid state objects that mutate one another's private fields or transition silently after a failed side effect. If behavior varies by a policy selected from outside and does not evolve through events, Strategy is the better model.

body:
Rule. State moves behavior that depends on an object's current mode into state-specific types behind one interface. The context delegates an event to its current state and installs the next state only after a valid transition. Use it when a lifecycle has several modes, repeated conditional logic, and meaningful invalid transitions.

Why it matters. A status enum is not a problem by itself. Trouble starts when controllers, services, and UI code each switch on that status and implement different transition rules. State objects put behavior and transition decisions together. They add types and indirection, so a small transition table may still be clearer as one explicit switch.

Worked example. Order 1001 begins Pending. pay(6000 cents) in Pending records payment and transitions to Paid. ship("TRACK-9") in Paid records the tracking number and transitions to Shipped. ship() in Pending returns InvalidTransition before calling the carrier. cancel() is allowed in Pending; in Paid it first requests a refund; in Shipped it is rejected because a return flow is required instead. Each state handles the same events but gives mode-specific results, and the Order context owns shared data such as id and total. Trace the happy path: Pending.pay → Paid.ship → Shipped. Trace a bad path: Pending.ship leaves the order Pending and produces no shipping side effect. If state is persisted as a status column, loading the order must restore the matching state object before the next event. A simple switch inside Order.handle(event) can express these four states well; move to separate state types when the handlers grow, vary independently, or are repeated elsewhere. This differs from Strategy: a caller usually chooses a sorting or pricing strategy, while an Order changes state because events occur during its own lifecycle.

[[diagram:states]]

[[diagram:transitions-png]]

When to use. Use State for protocols, workflow engines, order or document lifecycles, and UI modes where the same event means different things in different modes. Write the transition table first, make invalid moves explicit, and keep side effects coordinated with the state change so failures do not leave a false status.

When to refuse. Keep a boolean or enum when two modes have one small conditional. Do not create a class for every flag combination. Avoid state objects that mutate one another's private fields or transition silently after a failed side effect. If behavior varies by a policy selected from outside and does not evolve through events, Strategy is the better model.
